chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad, from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Ibrahim al-Kufi, from Al-Husayn ibn Zayd, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:
Rasool-Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'Give gifts with nabiq, so that cordiality and loyalty may live.'

key_terms.النَّبِقِ: A type of fruit or edible item, often identified as a small date or similar fruit, used here as a specific example of a gift.
key_terms.الْمَوَدَّةُ: Cordiality, deep affection, or love between individuals.
key_terms.الْمُوَالَاةُ: Loyalty, friendship, or mutual support and alliance.

ai.seo_question: What is the spiritual and social benefit of giving gifts in Islam according to hadith?
ai.summary: In this hadith from al-Kafi, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) narrates that the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him and his family) recommended exchanging 'nabiq' (often identified as a type of fig or sweet fruit) to cultivate mawaddah (affection) and muwalah (loyalty), reflecting the Shia emphasis on strengthening social bonds through tangible acts of generosity. This practice underscores the spiritual value of gift-giving not merely as a social courtesy but as a means of sustaining the covenant of love among the faithful, a concept deeply rooted in the Ahl al-Bayt's teachings on communal harmony.

en.hubeali:
Al Husayn Bin Muhammad, from Ja’far Bin Muhammad, from Abdul Rahman Bin Muhammad, from Muhammad Bin Ibrahim Al Kufy, from Al Husayn Bin Zayd, 
(It has been narrated) from Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> having said:
‘Rasool-Allah<sup>saww</sup> said: ‘Giving gifts with the fruit-bearing trees revives the cordiality and the loyalty’.
en.sarwar: 12. Ali ibn Ibrahim has narrated from his father from ibn abu ‘Umayr from Al-Nawfaliy from al-Sakuniy, who has said the following: “Abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, has said that Amir al-Mu’minin, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, has said, ‘Presenting a gift to my Muslim brother which can benefit him is more beloved to me than giving charity.’”
